screens.title: Distributed Tracing and Performance Monitoring with AWS X-Ray
screens.narratorSegment: In modern distributed systems a single user request can cross many services, containers, and functions. AWS X-Ray gives you the visibility to follow that request from end to end by recording segments for each compute resource and subsegments for the fine-grained calls inside them. On this lesson board you will learn what segments, subsegments, traces, and the service map are, how to instrument serverless and host-based applications using the X-Ray SDK and daemon, and how sampling rules let you control data volume and cost. We'll show concrete examples for a Python Lambda function, a CloudFormation snippet that installs the X-Ray daemon on EC2, and the CLI command to enable tracing on Lambda. You will also learn practical troubleshooting checks — for example, verifying that the SDK is configured to capture subsegments and the daemon is running — because missing one of these is the most common reason trace details are absent. By the end you'll understand how to use the service map and trace timeline to locate latency and error hotspots, and how to design sampling to capture important failures without sending every single request. Think about an intermittent 500 error—X-Ray helps you find which downstream call introduced it.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: This lesson has four concrete objectives that map to practical tasks you will perform with X-Ray. First, you will explain X-Ray's purpose and its core components so you can reason about traces, segments, and subsegments when you look at a service map. Second, you will instrument different application types — including Lambda, EC2, ECS, and A P I Gateway — which means enabling built-in tracing where available and installing the SDK and daemon where required. Third, you will use the service map and trace details to find performance bottlenecks and errors by reading timelines, durations, and included metadata. Finally, you will configure sampling rules to balance visibility against cost, learning about reservoirs and fixed rates so you capture important traces like authentication failures without tracing every single request. Each of these objectives is a competency you can demonstrate: reading a trace, adding SDK calls, verifying the daemon, and creating a sampling rule. These skills let you debug distributed latency and reduce mean time to resolution for production incidents.

screens.title: X-Ray core components: segments, subsegments, traces, service map
screens.narratorSegment: Let's define the primary components you will see in X-Ray and why each matters. A segment is a data record that represents work done by one compute resource — for example, a Lambda invocation, an EC2 process, or an ECS task. It captures timing, metadata, and exceptions for that resource. Subsegments live inside a segment and provide granular timing for specific operations such as a DynamoDB call, S3 access, or an external HTTP request. Together, a trace is the collection of segments and subsegments that share a common request identifier and represent the end-to-end path of a single request through your system. The service map aggregates traces to show nodes for services and edges for communication between them, colored to indicate health: green for healthy, yellow for warnings, and red for errors. These colors guide your investigation: a red edge points you to a flow that needs drilling down. A common misconception is thinking each segment always contains subsegments; in practice subsegments appear only when the SDK captures downstream calls or you explicitly create them. As you practice, make a habit of locating the trace ID first, then open the timeline to compare durations. The core insight is that segments give you resource-level context, subsegments give you operation-level context, and the service map gives you system-level context.

keyIdea.text: Segments are resource records, subsegments are internal operations, and traces connect them into a request timeline visible on the service map.

content.html:
Core Concept
Segments, Subsegments, Traces
Understand the building blocks of every trace and how they surface timing and metadata.
Segment
One compute resource's work record; includes duration, metadata, and exceptions.
Subsegment
Fine-grained operation timing inside a segment, created for SDK-wrapped calls or manual subsegments.
Trace
A collection of segments and subsegments sharing a trace ID representing the entire request path.
Key Takeaway

Use the trace ID to correlate segments across resources, and inspect subsegments to locate the exact operation causing latency or errors.

Service Map (visual)
Nodes represent services; edges represent connections and show aggregated health.
Color cues
Green = healthy, yellow = warnings, red = errors; use colors as a triage guide, not a definitive cause.
Drill down
Click a node or edge to open trace details and a timeline that shows durations for segments and subsegments.
Analogy
Think of a trace as a flight itinerary: segments are flights, subsegments are taxi, security, and baggage steps helping you pinpoint delays.

screens.title: Instrumenting managed services: Lambda, API Gateway, AppSync
screens.narratorSegment: Many managed AWS services can send trace data to X-Ray simply by toggling tracing on. For example, Lambda functions and A P I Gateway have a tracing configuration you can set to Active so the platform creates segments for each invocation. This is valuable because it requires no SDK changes and immediately populates the service map with nodes for those services. A concrete CLI example is enabling active tracing for a Lambda function using the update-function-configuration command; doing so causes Lambda to create the top-level segment for each invocation. A common misconception is that enabling tracing on Lambda alone will capture internal downstream calls automatically; it will create the Lambda segment, but downstream calls within your code may still require the X-Ray SDK or manual subsegments to record detailed timings and metadata. For A P I Gateway the trace will show incoming request timing and an edge to the backend; if the backend is a Lambda with active tracing, you will see a joined path in the service map. In practice, start by enabling tracing on managed services to get immediate visibility, then add the SDK in code paths where you need deeper subsegment detail.

keyIdea.title: Quick wins
keyIdea.text: Enable Active tracing on managed services for immediate segments; add SDK instrumentation later for deeper subsegment detail.

content.html:
Process Flow
Enable tracing on managed services
Turn on Active tracing for Lambda, API Gateway, and AppSync to generate segments automatically.
CLI example
aws lambda update-function-configuration \
    --function-name MyLambdaFunction \
    --tracing-config Mode=Active
When to add SDK
Add the X-Ray SDK where you need timing or metadata for downstream calls inside the function or service.
Common mistake

Assuming managed tracing replaces SDK instrumentation. It provides segments but not necessarily detailed subsegments for internal calls.

Practical check
After enabling tracing, invoke the service and confirm a trace appears in the X-Ray console for that resource.
Example: API Gateway + Lambda
Enable tracing on API Gateway and Lambda to see the edge between them and drill into the Lambda trace to inspect subsegments.
Why it matters
Immediate visibility reduces time-to-first-evidence when investigating production latency or errors.

screens.title: Python Lambda instrumentation with aws-xray-sdk
screens.narratorSegment: We'll walk through a concrete Python Lambda example using the aws-xray-sdk to create a segment for the Lambda invocation and subsegments for operations inside the handler. The example demonstrates capturing the handler with the recorder, creating a subsegment for an external A P I call, recording metadata like HTTP status, and creating an internal processing subsegment. When packaged and deployed with the sdk and any HTTP client library, the X-Ray daemon collects the segments and uploads them to the X-Ray service. A common practical issue is missing dependencies: the X-Ray SDK and an HTTP client must be present in the deployment package or supplied via a layer. Another common mistake is forgetting to mark exceptions or call add_error when handling failures; without marking an error, traces may not show that an operation failed. After deployment, invoke the function several times to see traces; look for the my underscore lambda underscore handler segment and the external underscore api underscore call and internal underscore processing subsegments in the trace timeline. Finally, check that the Lambda execution role includes the necessary write permissions or managed policies so traces can be uploaded successfully.

keyIdea.title: Instrumenting pattern
keyIdea.text: Wrap the handler with capture, create subsegments around important calls, and record metadata and errors to enrich traces.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
Python Lambda example
This handler shows capture and subsegments with metadata and error handling.
from aws_xray_sdk.core import xray_recorder
from aws_xray_sdk.core.lambda_launcher import LambdaContext

@xray_recorder.capture('my_lambda_handler')
def lambda_handler(event, context):
    print("Processing event:", event)

    # Simulate a delay
    import time
    time.sleep(0.05)

    # Create a subsegment for an external HTTP call
    with xray_recorder.in_subsegment('external_api_call') as subsegment:
        try:
            # Example HTTP client call
            import requests
            response = requests.get('https://docs.aws.amazon.com/index.html', timeout=2)
            subsegment.put_metadata('http_status', response.status_code)
            subsegment.put_metadata('response_length', len(response.text))
        except Exception as e:
            subsegment.add_exception(e)
            subsegment.add_error()

    # Internal processing
    with xray_recorder.in_subsegment('internal_processing'):
        time.sleep(0.03)

    return {
        'statusCode': 200,
        'body': 'X-Ray demo complete!'
    }
Packaging note
Include aws-xray-sdk and any HTTP clients in your deployment or use a Lambda Layer.
Runtime check
Invoke multiple times and inspect trace timeline for the handler segment and its subsegments.
Common mistakes
Missing dependencies, forgetting to add metadata or mark exceptions, and lacking IAM permissions are frequent causes of incomplete traces.
Key Takeaway

Capture the handler, create subsegments for important calls, and add metadata/errors so traces are actionable.

screens.title: Host-based instrumentation: X-Ray SDK and the X-Ray daemon
screens.narratorSegment: When applications run on EC2, ECS, or on-premises hosts, you must add two pieces: the X-Ray SDK in application code and the X-Ray daemon running nearby. The SDK instruments incoming requests and outgoing calls and sends segment data over UDP to the daemon. The daemon buffers that data and uploads it to the X-Ray service, handling batching and resilience. The daemon needs permission to write trace segments, so its IAM role or instance profile must include the managed policy for X-Ray daemon write access or the specific permissions xray:PutTraceSegments and xray:PutTelemetryRecords. The CloudFormation snippet in the chapter demonstrates creating an IAM role, instance profile, and user data that installs and starts the daemon. A common operational pitfall is placing the daemon on a different network path than the application or forgetting to set the AWS_XRAY_DAEMON_ADDRESS environment variable so the SDK can reach the daemon. Verify the daemon process is running and listening, then confirm traces upload in the console. The core principle is that the SDK creates segments locally and the daemon is the reliable uploader that converts local UDP packets into service-side traces.

keyIdea.title: Daemon role
keyIdea.text: The X-Ray daemon buffers SDK segment data and uploads it; it must run on the same host or reachable address and have proper IAM permissions.

content.html:
Architecture
X-Ray SDK + Daemon
SDK instruments and emits segments; the daemon buffers and uploads them to the X-Ray service.
Flow
Application → X-Ray SDK → UDP → X-Ray daemon → X-Ray service.
IAM requirement
Daemon's role needs xray:PutTraceSegments and xray:PutTelemetryRecords or the managed AWSXRayDaemonWriteAccess policy.
Operational tip

Ensure AWS_XRAY_DAEMON_ADDRESS points to the running daemon and that network/firewall rules allow UDP to the daemon port.

Example CloudFormation snippet (daemon role)
Resources:
  XRayDaemonRole:
    Type: AWS::IAM::Role
    Properties:
      AssumeRolePolicyDocument: ...
      ManagedPolicyArns:
        - arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AWSXRayDaemonWriteAccess

  XRayInstanceProfile:
    Type: AWS::IAM::InstanceProfile
    Properties:
      Roles:
        - !Ref XRayDaemonRole

  MyEC2Instance:
    Type: AWS::EC2::Instance
    Properties:
      IamInstanceProfile: !Ref XRayInstanceProfile
      UserData: |
        # install and start the X-Ray daemon
Checklist
  • Install and start the daemon on the host.
  • Set SDK environment variables to reach the daemon.
  • Confirm IAM role includes X-Ray write permissions.

screens.title: Service map and trace details: diagnosing latency and errors
screens.narratorSegment: The service map is your system-level triage tool. It aggregates traces and draws nodes for services and edges for traffic between them, with colors reflecting aggregated health. When you see a red edge it tells you there are frequent errors on that path; yellow suggests elevated latency or occasional warnings. The trace details provide the evidence: a timeline where each segment and subsegment is shown with duration, start time, and any metadata or exceptions attached. To diagnose a slow A P I request, start at the service map and click the slow edge to view individual traces. In the trace timeline, look for the largest horizontal block — that operation added the most latency. For example, an A P I Gateway showing high latency may reveal a Lambda segment where a DynamoDB subsegment is the dominant delay. Always check metadata and HTTP status codes in the subsegment to confirm whether the slowness is due to retries, a cold start, a misconfigured query, or an external A P I. A common misconception is to assume color alone indicates root cause; colors are a guide — the timeline and metadata reveal the true cause.

keyIdea.title: Diagnose with evidence
keyIdea.text: Use the service map to triage, then read trace timelines and metadata to identify the exact operation causing latency or errors.

content.html:
Definition
Service map and trace details
Use the map to find hotspots and the trace timeline to confirm the root cause.
Service map cues
  • Green nodes: healthy.
  • Yellow edges: potential latency or warnings.
  • Red edges: frequent errors needing immediate attention.
Misconception

Don't treat colors as proof. Drill into trace timelines and metadata for the true cause.

Trace timeline analysis
Look for the longest segment/subsegment, inspect metadata and exception details, and correlate HTTP codes or DB duration to determine root cause.
Scenario
API shows high latency. Trace reveals Lambda segment with DynamoDB subsegment taking most time and returning throttling errors in metadata. Conclusion: optimize the DynamoDB query or add retries with backoff.

screens.title: Sampling rules: reservoir and fixed rate
screens.narratorSegment: Sampling rules are how you control the amount of trace data X-Ray ingests. By default X-Ray keeps one request per second and samples five percent of additional requests. Custom sampling rules let you change that behavior with two main controls: the reservoir and the fixed rate. A reservoir is a small per-second allotment that guarantees a fixed number of traces every second, useful for ensuring some coverage even under heavy load. The fixed rate is the percentage of additional requests that should be traced. Use these together to capture all traffic for critical endpoints while sampling less for noisy, low-value paths. For example, trace 100 percent of requests to a login endpoint by setting its fixed rate to 1.0 or reserving a suitable reservoir while setting low fixed rates for health-check paths. When designing sampling, test the effect on trace counts and costs: over-sampling increases ingestion and cost, under-sampling may hide intermittent failures. A practical misconception is relying only on default sampling; for production systems you should explicitly define rules for critical endpoints and errors to guarantee visibility when it matters most.

keyIdea.title: Sampling strategy
keyIdea.text: Use reservoir to guarantee a minimum number of traces and fixed rate to tune percentages, prioritizing critical endpoints and error conditions.

content.html:
Process Flow
Sampling rules
Define reservoirs and fixed rates to balance visibility and cost.
Key terms
  • Reservoir: fixed number of traces per second guaranteed.
  • FixedRate: percentage of additional requests to trace.
Rule example (conceptual)
{
  "RuleName": "LoginHighSampling",
  "Reservoir": 1,
  "FixedRate": 1.0,
  "MatchConditions": { "URLPath": "/login" }
}
This conceptual block shows reserving traces and setting full sampling for a critical path.
Key Takeaway

Start with conservative sampling and increase coverage only for specific endpoints or error conditions that require full visibility.

screens.title: Common mistakes and troubleshooting checklist
screens.narratorSegment: When traces appear in X-Ray but lack subsegments or metadata, there are a few recurring root causes to check in a predictable order. First, confirm the X-Ray SDK is installed and configured to capture the types of downstream calls you expect. Many SDKs require explicit wrapping of HTTP or AWS SDK calls to create subsegments. Second, ensure the X-Ray daemon is running and reachable; the SDK sends UDP packets to the daemon, so if the daemon is not running or the address is misconfigured, segments will not be uploaded. Third, check IAM permissions: the daemon or execution role must have xray:PutTraceSegments and xray:PutTelemetryRecords or use the managed daemon write policy. Fourth, verify sampling rules; aggressive sampling can drop traces that would otherwise include subsegments. The assessment question in the chapter highlights a typical scenario where traces exist but lack subsegments because the SDK was not configured correctly to capture downstream calls. The troubleshooting approach is to replicate a failing request, capture logs from the daemon and SDK, and correct the missing configuration. This ordered checklist reduces guesswork and helps you restore full trace fidelity quickly.

narration.text: When traces appear in X-Ray but lack subsegments or metadata, there are a few recurring root causes to check in a predictable order. First, confirm the X-Ray SDK is installed and configured to capture the types of downstream calls you expect. Many SDKs require explicit wrapping of HTTP or AWS SDK calls to create subsegments. Second, ensure the X-Ray daemon is running and reachable; the SDK sends UDP packets to the daemon, so if the daemon is not running or the address is misconfigured, segments will not be uploaded. Third, check IAM permissions: the daemon or execution role must have xray:PutTraceSegments and xray:PutTelemetryRecords or use the managed daemon write policy. Fourth, verify sampling rules; aggressive sampling can drop traces that would otherwise include subsegments. The assessment question in the chapter highlights a typical scenario where traces exist but lack subsegments because the SDK was not configured correctly to capture downstream calls. The troubleshooting approach is to replicate a failing request, capture logs from the daemon and SDK, and correct the missing configuration. This ordered checklist reduces guesswork and helps you restore full trace fidelity quickly.

keyIdea.text: Check SDK configuration, daemon availability, IAM permissions, and sampling rules in that order to restore missing trace details.

content.html:
Comparison
Why traces are incomplete
A short checklist compares likely root causes and fixes.
Cause: Missing SDK config
Fix: Wrap downstream calls or enable automatic instrumentation for AWS SDKs so subsegments are created.
Cause: Daemon not running
Fix: Start the X-Ray daemon on host or set AWS_XRAY_DAEMON_ADDRESS to a reachable host and port.
Cause: IAM permissions
Fix: Ensure the daemon or task role has X-Ray write permissions such as the AWSXRayDaemonWriteAccess policy.
Cause: Sampling rules
Fix: Adjust sampling rules to increase coverage for the affected endpoints or error classes.
Pro tip

Replicate an issue with verbose SDK and daemon logs to quickly identify whether data is emitted, collected, or uploaded.

content.html:
Hands-on Activity
Instrument and analyze
Follow these steps to verify traces appear end to end.
1. Create Lambda and role
Ensure the execution role includes X-Ray write permissions like AWSXRayDaemonWriteAccess.
2. Deploy code with aws-xray-sdk
Package dependencies or use a layer for aws-xray-sdk and any HTTP client library.
3. Enable Active tracing
aws lambda update-function-configuration --function-name XRayDemoFunction --tracing-config Mode=Active
4. Invoke and inspect
Invoke several times, open X-Ray Traces, and inspect timeline and metadata for subsegments.
Example Lambda snippet
from aws_xray_sdk.core import xray_recorder
@xray_recorder.capture('my_lambda_handler')
def lambda_handler(event, context):
    with xray_recorder.in_subsegment('internal_processing'):
        import time
        time.sleep(0.03)
    return {'statusCode':200,'body':'X-Ray demo complete!'}
Key Takeaway

Validate traces after each change: code, packaging, permissions, and configuration are common failure points.

screens.title: Sampling and cost optimization best practices
screens.narratorSegment: Balancing observability and cost is a core operational challenge. Start tracing with conservative global rates then identify critical paths to increase sampling. Prioritize error traces by creating sampling rules that target HTTP 5xx status codes or endpoints that perform authentication and financial transactions. Use reservoirs to guarantee a minimal number of traces per second for key services during spikes. Roll out deeper instrumentation gradually: enable managed tracing first, then add SDK subsegments for high-value operations. Monitor trace ingestion and billing closely after changes so you can back off if costs rise. Remember that over-sampling can quickly increase ingestion, while under-sampling can hide intermittent, high-impact failures. A practical rollout plan is to enable tracing in staging with higher sampling, validate trace usefulness, then apply tuned rules in production. Always include metadata and exception markers in your subsegments so sampled traces are maximally informative. The final takeaway is to treat sampling as a safety valve: it protects cost while letting you design rules that capture the traces you actually need to resolve incidents. Best Practices
Sampling and cost optimization
A practical guide to choose rates and roll out tracing safely.
Start conservative
Begin with low global rates and increase for specific endpoints after validating value.
Prioritize errors
Create rules to capture 100% of error traffic or set higher fixed rates for 5xx responses.
Use reservoirs
Guarantee some traces per second during spikes for critical services to avoid blind spots.
Key Takeaway

Design sampling rules around business-critical paths and error conditions, validate in staging, and monitor ingestion trends to balance visibility and cost.

fullNarratorScript:
In modern distributed systems a single user request can cross many services, containers, and functions. AWS X-Ray gives you the visibility to follow that request from end to end by recording segments for each compute resource and subsegments for the fine-grained calls inside them. On this lesson board you will learn what segments, subsegments, traces, and the service map are, how to instrument serverless and host-based applications using the X-Ray SDK and daemon, and how sampling rules let you control data volume and cost. We'll show concrete examples for a Python Lambda function, a CloudFormation snippet that installs the X-Ray daemon on EC2, and the CLI command to enable tracing on Lambda. You will also learn practical troubleshooting checks — for example, verifying that the SDK is configured to capture subsegments and the daemon is running — because missing one of these is the most common reason trace details are absent. By the end you'll understand how to use the service map and trace timeline to locate latency and error hotspots, and how to design sampling to capture important failures without sending every single request. Think about an intermittent 500 error—X-Ray helps you find which downstream call introduced it.

This lesson has four concrete objectives that map to practical tasks you will perform with X-Ray. First, you will explain X-Ray's purpose and its core components so you can reason about traces, segments, and subsegments when you look at a service map. Second, you will instrument different application types — including Lambda, EC2, ECS, and A P I Gateway — which means enabling built-in tracing where available and installing the SDK and daemon where required. Third, you will use the service map and trace details to find performance bottlenecks and errors by reading timelines, durations, and included metadata. Finally, you will configure sampling rules to balance visibility against cost, learning about reservoirs and fixed rates so you capture important traces like authentication failures without tracing every single request. Each of these objectives is a competency you can demonstrate: reading a trace, adding SDK calls, verifying the daemon, and creating a sampling rule. These skills let you debug distributed latency and reduce mean time to resolution for production incidents.

Now that the objectives are clear, let's link each to a practical competency. For explaining components, practice by reading a trace: identify a segment, find its subsegments, and confirm the trace ID that ties them together. For instrumentation, demonstrate enabling X-Ray on a Lambda and adding the X-Ray SDK and daemon on an EC2 instance, then verify traces appear in the console. For analysis, perform a drill-down from the service map into a slow edge and read the trace timeline to find which subsegment added the most milliseconds. For sampling, implement a rule that traces 100% of a critical endpoint and a lower fixed rate for noncritical ones; verify how the trace count changes. These are measurable skills. When you perform each task, verify the expected result: segments created for each compute resource, subsegments for downstream calls, trace entries appearing in the X-Ray console, and sampling changes reducing trace volume. Practicing these steps builds muscle memory so you can respond quickly to incidents in production.

Let's define the primary components you will see in X-Ray and why each matters. A segment is a data record that represents work done by one compute resource — for example, a Lambda invocation, an EC2 process, or an ECS task. It captures timing, metadata, and exceptions for that resource. Subsegments live inside a segment and provide granular timing for specific operations such as a DynamoDB call, S3 access, or an external HTTP request. Together, a trace is the collection of segments and subsegments that share a common request identifier and represent the end-to-end path of a single request through your system. The service map aggregates traces to show nodes for services and edges for communication between them, colored to indicate health: green for healthy, yellow for warnings, and red for errors. These colors guide your investigation: a red edge points you to a flow that needs drilling down. A common misconception is thinking each segment always contains subsegments; in practice subsegments appear only when the SDK captures downstream calls or you explicitly create them. As you practice, make a habit of locating the trace ID first, then open the timeline to compare durations. The core insight is that segments give you resource-level context, subsegments give you operation-level context, and the service map gives you system-level context.

Many managed AWS services can send trace data to X-Ray simply by toggling tracing on. For example, Lambda functions and A P I Gateway have a tracing configuration you can set to Active so the platform creates segments for each invocation. This is valuable because it requires no SDK changes and immediately populates the service map with nodes for those services. A concrete CLI example is enabling active tracing for a Lambda function using the update-function-configuration command; doing so causes Lambda to create the top-level segment for each invocation. A common misconception is that enabling tracing on Lambda alone will capture internal downstream calls automatically; it will create the Lambda segment, but downstream calls within your code may still require the X-Ray SDK or manual subsegments to record detailed timings and metadata. For A P I Gateway the trace will show incoming request timing and an edge to the backend; if the backend is a Lambda with active tracing, you will see a joined path in the service map. In practice, start by enabling tracing on managed services to get immediate visibility, then add the SDK in code paths where you need deeper subsegment detail.

We'll walk through a concrete Python Lambda example using the aws-xray-sdk to create a segment for the Lambda invocation and subsegments for operations inside the handler. The example demonstrates capturing the handler with the recorder, creating a subsegment for an external A P I call, recording metadata like HTTP status, and creating an internal processing subsegment. When packaged and deployed with the sdk and any HTTP client library, the X-Ray daemon collects the segments and uploads them to the X-Ray service. A common practical issue is missing dependencies: the X-Ray SDK and an HTTP client must be present in the deployment package or supplied via a layer. Another common mistake is forgetting to mark exceptions or call add_error when handling failures; without marking an error, traces may not show that an operation failed. After deployment, invoke the function several times to see traces; look for the my underscore lambda underscore handler segment and the external underscore api underscore call and internal underscore processing subsegments in the trace timeline. Finally, check that the Lambda execution role includes the necessary write permissions or managed policies so traces can be uploaded successfully.

When applications run on EC2, ECS, or on-premises hosts, you must add two pieces: the X-Ray SDK in application code and the X-Ray daemon running nearby. The SDK instruments incoming requests and outgoing calls and sends segment data over UDP to the daemon. The daemon buffers that data and uploads it to the X-Ray service, handling batching and resilience. The daemon needs permission to write trace segments, so its IAM role or instance profile must include the managed policy for X-Ray daemon write access or the specific permissions xray:PutTraceSegments and xray:PutTelemetryRecords. The CloudFormation snippet in the chapter demonstrates creating an IAM role, instance profile, and user data that installs and starts the daemon. A common operational pitfall is placing the daemon on a different network path than the application or forgetting to set the AWS_XRAY_DAEMON_ADDRESS environment variable so the SDK can reach the daemon. Verify the daemon process is running and listening, then confirm traces upload in the console. The core principle is that the SDK creates segments locally and the daemon is the reliable uploader that converts local UDP packets into service-side traces.

The service map is your system-level triage tool. It aggregates traces and draws nodes for services and edges for traffic between them, with colors reflecting aggregated health. When you see a red edge it tells you there are frequent errors on that path; yellow suggests elevated latency or occasional warnings. The trace details provide the evidence: a timeline where each segment and subsegment is shown with duration, start time, and any metadata or exceptions attached. To diagnose a slow A P I request, start at the service map and click the slow edge to view individual traces. In the trace timeline, look for the largest horizontal block — that operation added the most latency. For example, an A P I Gateway showing high latency may reveal a Lambda segment where a DynamoDB subsegment is the dominant delay. Always check metadata and HTTP status codes in the subsegment to confirm whether the slowness is due to retries, a cold start, a misconfigured query, or an external A P I. A common misconception is to assume color alone indicates root cause; colors are a guide — the timeline and metadata reveal the true cause.

Sampling rules are how you control the amount of trace data X-Ray ingests. By default X-Ray keeps one request per second and samples five percent of additional requests. Custom sampling rules let you change that behavior with two main controls: the reservoir and the fixed rate. A reservoir is a small per-second allotment that guarantees a fixed number of traces every second, useful for ensuring some coverage even under heavy load. The fixed rate is the percentage of additional requests that should be traced. Use these together to capture all traffic for critical endpoints while sampling less for noisy, low-value paths. For example, trace 100 percent of requests to a login endpoint by setting its fixed rate to 1.0 or reserving a suitable reservoir while setting low fixed rates for health-check paths. When designing sampling, test the effect on trace counts and costs: over-sampling increases ingestion and cost, under-sampling may hide intermittent failures. A practical misconception is relying only on default sampling; for production systems you should explicitly define rules for critical endpoints and errors to guarantee visibility when it matters most.

Fourth, verify sampling rules; aggressive sampling can drop traces that would otherwise include subsegments. This ordered checklist reduces guesswork and helps you restore full trace fidelity quickly.
